how-much-to-charge-per-window.html.text:
← Open the calculator

How much should a window cleaner charge per window?

A stranger typing that query wants a number. The honest answer is that a single number is how operators lose money. After using the method below, you can name a visit price from your own times and costs, which used to take a guess plus a flyer you copied from a competitor.

What a per-window flyer cannot see

Ten ground-floor plates on a water-fed pole are not the same job as ten French panes, both sides, on a third story. The flyer prices them the same. The third-story French job is often three to four times the labor. If you also drove 25 minutes and spent ten more getting the hose up, a six-pane ranch at $8 a window is a $48 invoice for most of an hour of paid time plus fuel.

The arithmetic

  1. Split the glass. Count panes by type, not by “windows” on the elevation. A sliding door is not a bathroom hopper.
  2. Time one side. Minutes per pane are per side. Interior plus exterior is two sides. French or divided lights take longer because each light is work.
  3. Add the drive. Travel and setup do not shrink when the pane count does. That is why a minimum job charge exists.
  4. Load the wage. The number on the paycheck is not the cost of an hour. Employer taxes, workers’ compensation, and insurance sit on top.
  5. Price from cost. Direct cost plus overhead, then divide by (1 − the margin you intend to keep). If that is below your minimum, the minimum wins.
  6. Only then divide by panes if you want a per-window figure to quote. It is an output, not an input.

The window cleaning bid calculator is that method with the numbers filled in. Starting minutes are ballpark figures, not a standard. Replace them with times from your own stops.

Residential vs commercial

Residential is usually one visit; the travel block is a large share of the invoice. Commercial is the same visit math times visits per month. A storefront that looks “cheap per window” is often 8 minutes a plate every week — a labor hour hiding inside a $15 pane.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own costs before submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

FOR WINDOW CLEANING OPERATORS

Price the stop, not the pane count.

A flat “per window” quote cannot see that ten French panes both sides are a different job from ten ground-floor plates, or that a 25-minute drive does not shrink when the house is small. Time each glass type, add travel and setup, load the wage, and see the visit price, the price per pane, and the number below which the stop loses money.

The glass

One row per glass type. Minutes are per pane on one side — pick a type to start from a common figure, then replace it with a time from your own stops. Sides: 1 is in-only or out-only; 2 is both.

Glass typePanesMin / paneSides

Your costs

Travel and setup is the block that sinks small jobs: drive, park, hose-up, and pack-out happen once whether the house has 8 panes or 80. The minimum job charge exists to cover that block. Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, and insurance — underestimating it is the other common miss.

A bid link carries every glass type and your own rates — wage, burden, overhead, and target margin — so the page reopens exactly as you left it. Send it to yourself or a second estimator. The customer should get the price, not the link.

Where the pane labor goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting minutes are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own stops and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    How much should I charge per window?

    A flat per-window price hides travel and glass type. Time each pane type, add the drive and setup, load the wage, then divide the visit price by pane count. Ten French panes both sides are a different job from ten ground-floor plates.

    Why do small window cleaning jobs lose money?

    Travel and setup do not shrink when the pane count does. A 25-minute drive plus hose-up on an 8-pane ranch is mostly windshield time. A minimum job charge exists to cover that block, not to pad profit.

    How do I price interior and exterior together?

    Count sides. One side is exterior-only or interior-only. Two sides is in and out. Minutes per pane stay per side, so a French pane at 4 minutes both sides is 8 minutes of glass before you have moved to the next one.

    How much more should I charge for second-story, lift, or hard-water windows?

    The calculator’s own starting figures show the jump: ground-floor exterior on a water-fed pole starts at 1.5 minutes per pane. A second-story ladder job starts at 3 minutes — double. Third-story, bosun-chair, or lift work starts at 6 minutes, four times the ground-floor figure, because rigging and safety add time before the glass gets touched. Hard-water or restoration glass and skylights both start at 8 minutes per pane — over five times the base rate — since mineral deposits need a chemical pass or a second wipe regardless of how reachable the glass is. Pick the preset closest to the access and glass condition in front of you, then replace it with a time from your own stopwatch; these are starting points for the group, not a published rate for the trade.

vs-a-flat-price-per-window.html.text:
← Window Cleaning Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per window

A price per window is the number homeowners and storefront managers ask for — $5 a window, $6 a pane, "we beat any quote." That rate cannot see glass type or the drive, and the same rate that clears a profit on a ground-floor house loses money outright on French panes or storefront plate.

What a flat price per window is

It is the fastest number to quote over the phone: one rate, times the window count, whatever the glass turns out to be when the cleaner arrives. It is learned on a stop that was easy to price — usually ground-floor exterior panes on a water-fed pole — and then quoted again on the next job that calls.

Nothing about "how many windows" tells the operator whether those windows are ground-floor plates or French panes cleaned both sides, or how far the van has to drive to reach them. The flat rate does not ask, because it was never built to answer.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter one row per glass type — pane count, minutes per pane, and sides — plus travel minutes and your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It prices the visit from what this specific glass and this specific drive actually cost, not a rate learned on the last stop.

What a flat price per window doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate per window for ground-floor exterior glass and French panes cleaned both sides, even though the French panes can take five to six times as long. Prices each glass type from its own pane count, minutes per pane, and sides, so a harder mix costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for sides — interior-and-exterior work on the same pane count gets the same rate as exterior-only. Multiplies minutes by sides per glass-type row, so in-and-out work is priced as the two passes it actually is.
Has no line for travel — a 10-minute hop and a 45-minute drive get the same rate. Prices travel and setup minutes separately, and reports travel's share of the visit so a short stop cannot hide that most of the invoice is the drive.
Gives the operator a number to quote over the phone before the glass has been seen, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the break-even cost and the price at your target margin, so a flat rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.
Cannot tell you when the flat rate is a loss rather than a thin margin. Prices the job from its own inputs, so a rate that undercuts cost shows up as a negative margin instead of a surprise at month-end.

Same window count, two different jobs

Two 50-window stops, priced from this calculator's own arithmetic with a $20 hourly wage, 25% payroll burden, $8 supplies and $12 other cost per visit, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin — no minimum job charge, so the numbers below are the real cost-and-margin price, not a floor.

StopGlassCostThis calculator's priceReal per-window rate
A — ground-floor house50 ground-floor exterior panes, 20-min drive$68.52$85.65$1.71
B — French & storefront job30 French panes (both sides) + 20 storefront plate-glass panes, 20-min drive$224.25$280.31$5.61

Quote Stop B at the per-window rate learned from Stop A — $1.71 a window, times 50 windows — and the total comes to $85.65. Stop B actually costs $224.25 to run. That flat quote is $138.60 under cost, not a thin margin: every visit at that rate loses money before overhead or profit are even counted. The two stops have the identical window count; only the glass differs.

When to still just quote a flat rate

If a route only ever sees one kind of glass — a subdivision of similar ground-floor houses, say — a flat per-window number can land close to cost, because the glass mix genuinely does not vary from stop to stop. The risk is the call that is not like the others: French panes, a second-story or lift job, or a storefront with plate glass, quoted at the same rate because the phone call never asked what kind of windows they were.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per window get a bid wrong?

Because the rate is learned on one kind of glass -- usually easy ground-floor exterior panes -- and then quoted on the next job sight unseen, whatever the glass turns out to be. This calculator's own arithmetic prices 50 ground-floor exterior panes at a real per-window rate of $1.71 once travel and margin are counted. Quote that same $1.71 a window on 50 French and storefront panes and the total comes to $85.65 against a job that actually costs $224.25 to run -- a $138.60 loss, not a thin margin, on a job this calculator prices at $280.31.

What does a flat per-window rate usually miss entirely?

Glass type and sides (a French or divided-light pane cleaned both sides can take five to six times as long as a ground-floor exterior plate on a water-fed pole), and travel and setup, which do not shrink because the stop is small. A flat rate has no line for either -- it is one number learned on one kind of stop and reused for the next job that calls, regardless of the glass or the drive.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own cost inputs -- $20 hourly wage, 25% burden, $8 supplies and $12 other cost per visit, 15% overhead, 20% target margin: 50 ground-floor exterior panes with a 20-minute drive cost $68.52 to run and price at $85.65 with no minimum charge applied. 50 panes split between French (both sides) and storefront plate glass, same 20-minute drive, cost $224.25 to run and price at $280.31. Quoting the second job at the first job's per-window rate ($1.71) comes to $85.65 -- $138.60 under the actual cost, not just under the target price.

Is a flat per-window rate ever a reasonable shorthand?

For stops that stay to one glass type -- a whole house of ground-floor exterior, say -- a flat number can land close to cost. The risk is quoting French panes, second-story or lift access, or storefront plate glass at that same rate over the phone, because the advertised rate does not know the glass mix until the cleaner is already looking at the windows.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or glass pricing?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or what a competitor charges. It takes the pane count, minutes per pane, and sides for each glass type on the stop, plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel minutes, supplies, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this visit -- the arithmetic a flat per-window rate skips, not a market survey.

Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, drive time, and supply costs, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

vs-servicemonster.html.text:
← Window Cleaning Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. ServiceMonster

Two different shapes: ServiceMonster is account-based field-service management software for running a window cleaning company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one visit cost, given its panes, glass type, and travel, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceMonster is field-service management software that markets specifically to cleaning-industry businesses — window cleaning, pressure washing, carpet cleaning, and related exterior and interior cleaning trades. Its roots go back to 2002 as software built for carpet cleaners, and it is headquartered in Bellingham, Washington. It combines customer and account management, job scheduling and technician routing, estimates and invoicing, and automated marketing campaigns into one subscription system, with a mobile app for crews in the field. ServiceMonster's own marketing says it is trusted by thousands of service pros, and industry coverage reports it was acquired in 2023 by Teamfront. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. ServiceMonster's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — cleaning-industry field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceMonster appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceMonster does. It does not manage customer accounts, route technicians across a schedule, or run marketing campaigns, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one visit's panes, grouped by glass type — ground-floor, French or divided-light, second- and third-story access, storefront plate, skylights, screens, and hard-water or restoration glass — with minutes per pane and sides, plus travel and setup time, cleaner wage, payroll burden, supplies, fuel, overhead, target margin, and a minimum job charge, and turns that into the per-visit price, the price per pane, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the visit loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one stop. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Most window cleaning operators get different value from each: ServiceMonster (or a comparable field-service platform) for running customer accounts, routing, scheduling, and marketing across a whole company as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on what one stop should cost from its panes and access before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed proposal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ServiceMonster?

They do different jobs, and a window cleaning company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. ServiceMonster is field-service management software built for cleaning-industry businesses — it markets specifically to window cleaning, pressure washing, and carpet cleaning companies, and has roots going back to 2002 as carpet-cleaning-industry software, headquartered in Bellingham, Washington. It combines customer and account management, scheduling and routing, estimates and invoicing, and automated marketing campaigns into one subscription system, and it says it is trusted by thousands of service pros. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account, and industry coverage reports it was acquired in 2023 by Teamfront. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from panes grouped by glass type — ground-floor, French or divided-light, second- and third-story access, storefront, skylights, screens, and hard-water or restoration glass — with minutes per pane and sides, plus travel and setup, loaded wage, supplies, fuel, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the per-visit price, the price per pane, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the visit loses money, before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A window cleaning company that already manages accounts, routing, and marketing campaigns across every crew and every stop is better served by ServiceMonster or a comparable field-service platform; a cleaner who wants an instant, private gut-check on what one stop should cost from its pane count and access before opening a business system is in the right place here.
